why_it_remains_plausible: One ordinary or utility-QoS busy child is enough to move the no-op timer into the fast band, while background and maintenance QoS CPU remain slow despite consuming CPU.
current_constraints: Generic CPU load is ruled out, and adding more ordinary busy children is not monotonically better.
counter_or_trace_contract: Capture per-core residency, cluster frequency, package power, and renderer process/core placement for no-op, ordinary CPU, nice CPU, utility CPU, taskpolicy -b, QoS background, QoS maintenance, and finite-burst gap-decay rows.
would_support_if: Fast rows share higher performance-cluster residency or frequency during the keydown/EventDispatch window, and finite-burst rows decay as that state decays.
would_weaken_if: Fast and slow QoS rows have the same frequency/residency and renderer placement during the measured key window.

why_it_remains_plausible: The fast/slow split follows ordinary/utility versus background/maintenance policy more closely than Unix nice or taskpolicy latency/throughput tiers.
current_constraints: `nice +20` remains fast; taskpolicy latency and throughput tiers remain fast; `taskpolicy -b`, QoS background, and QoS maintenance remain slow.
counter_or_trace_contract: Use Instruments System Trace or equivalent to record thread QoS, runnable-to-running latency, context switches, core IDs, and scheduler priority for the browser renderer, GPU/compositor if relevant, and helper CPU processes.
would_support_if: Fast rows show lower renderer scheduling latency, different core placement, or different effective QoS/priority during key dispatch even when helper CPU duration is matched.
would_weaken_if: Renderer scheduling latency and effective QoS are indistinguishable across ordinary/utility and background/maintenance controls.

why_it_remains_plausible: Recent CPU work lowers the measured Gutenberg input slice, and the broad Gutenberg path has thousands of small JS/data/RichText calls that could be sensitive to cache or memory latency.
current_constraints: External child CPU and worker CPU can move the path, so the explanation cannot require warming Gutenberg-specific JS objects directly.
counter_or_trace_contract: Collect renderer cycles, instructions, cache misses, branch misses if available, and task-level CPU time around the same EventDispatch window for matched finite-burst and continuous-QoS rows.
would_support_if: Fast rows show lower renderer stall or miss rate during EventDispatch without a matching scheduler/frequency difference.
would_weaken_if: Renderer hardware-counter ratios are the same across fast and slow rows, or differences follow frequency/scheduling instead.

why_it_remains_plausible: Finite CPU recency matters, and OS policy can change timer and wakeup behavior.
current_constraints: The measured movement is EventDispatch duration, not only time from timer/key scheduling to dispatch start; near-key no-CPU timers and delays stay slow.
counter_or_trace_contract: Align timer fire time, helper work start/end, next keydown enqueue, EventDispatch start, and renderer thread wakeups with OS wakeup and timer-coalescing records.
would_support_if: Fast rows primarily reduce key enqueue-to-EventDispatch-start or renderer wakeup latency, with little change inside the EventDispatch work itself.
would_weaken_if: EventDispatch starts at comparable times but its internal JS/data/RichText work duration changes.

why_it_remains_plausible: Browser/runtime checkpoints and CPU/QoS controls both show that work charged to EventDispatch depends on state below Gutenberg selectors.
current_constraints: Current Chromium render traces capture visual pipeline endpoints, not scheduler state for task queues or input budgets.
counter_or_trace_contract: Record Chromium scheduler/task-queue categories, renderer main-thread task boundaries, input task priority, V8 slices, and Gutenberg source spans in the same key windows used by the CPU/QoS controls.
would_support_if: Fast rows show different input-task priority, queueing, or task splitting while OS counters alone do not explain the split.
would_weaken_if: Browser scheduler traces are identical once OS frequency/residency/QoS counters are controlled.

why_it_remains_plausible: Native contenteditable moves by less than 1ms while Gutenberg moves by many milliseconds, so source fanout supplies the scale.
current_constraints: System state modulates the benchmarked path but does not identify a safe Gutenberg code change.
counter_or_trace_contract: Keep selector/subscriber prototypes and workload replay separate from OS-counter experiments; use the same source spans only to confirm product-scale amplification.
would_support_if: Source prototypes reduce the broad input work across both slow and fast system states.
would_weaken_if: Source changes only change the artifact under one system policy and regress behavior or workload replay.
